title: The Long Machine
premise: Astrid Kavanagh investigates impossible insurance claims on Meridian, a failing colony whose records keep quietly rewriting themselves. When the deep-space vessel Halcyon returns with its crew aged backward into children, Astrid discovers the ship is a memory engine built from his own family's stolen inheritance, and that a massacre aboard it has been edited out of every archive. To prove what happened, he must feed his own memories into the machine, risking erasure. In the end he restores the truth to the colony's record at the cost of forgetting his mother's face, and chooses to stay among people who finally remember him.
about_author: B. M. Dunmore is the pen name of a former maritime claims adjuster who spent eleven years investigating losses at sea before turning to fiction. They write slow-burning science fiction about paperwork, grief, and machines that remember too much.

chapters.title: Actuarial
chapters.summary: POV Astrid. On dying colony Meridian, Astrid closes out another impossible claim: a greenhouse that burned without heat signatures. His supervisor urges him to stop noticing patterns in the archives that contradict themselves. The beat is quiet loneliness; Astrid keeps meticulous personal journals because no one else remembers anything accurately.

chapters.title: The Return of Halcyon
chapters.summary: POV Astrid. A ship thought lost forty years ago docks with a crew of children wearing adult ranks and memories. One child, Captain Okafor aged nine, recognizes Astrid by name though they've never met. The beat is uncanny wonder curdling into dread as the port authority seals the ship and forbids investigation.

chapters.title: Paper Ghosts
chapters.summary: POV Astrid. Astrid pulls the Halcyon's original manifest and finds his grandmother listed as chief engineer, though family legend says she died planetbound. Records of the voyage exist in triplicate, all identical, all wrong. Beat: obsessive hope, the first taste of inheritance as a mystery rather than a gift.

chapters.title: Children of the Voyage
chapters.summary: POV Okafor (child-captain). Inside quarantine, the regressed crew experiences flashes of an event none can name: screaming, a corridor flooding with light, orders to forget. Okafor hides a scorched logbook sliver. Beat: fractured memory as both wound and evidence, trust slowly extended to Astrid through the glass.

chapters.title: The Kavanagh Clause
chapters.summary: POV Astrid. Astrid finds his grandmother's patent filings for a mnemonic drive that stores human memory as fuel, sold off under coercion to the colonial consortium. Every impossible claim he ever investigated traces back to memory 'withdrawals.' Beat: fury and vertigo as his career reframes as complicity.

chapters.title: What the Water Kept
chapters.summary: POV Astrid. Following the logbook sliver, Astrid and Okafor locate the drowned original settlement where the first prototype ran. Submerged ruins hold a memorial wall naming two hundred dead colonists who officially never existed. Beat: mourning made physical; belonging to a place that was erased alongside its people.

chapters.title: Amendment Seven
chapters.summary: POV Consortium auditor Vey. The antagonist chapter: Vey arrives to liquidate Meridian and sanitize the Halcyon, revealing the massacre was a deliberate purge of witnesses to the drive's fuel source. Vey offers Astrid wealth and restored memories if he signs off. Beat: temptation framed as mercy; Astrid refuses.

chapters.title: Fuel
chapters.summary: POV Astrid. The crew plans to broadcast the truth via the drive itself, but it needs living memory as charge. Astrid volunteers his journals and his mind, knowing the process consumes what it takes. Okafor begs him not to. Beat: sacrifice chosen freely; the theme of inheritance turned literal.

chapters.title: The Massacre, Proven
chapters.summary: POV multiple, braided during the broadcast. The drive floods every screen on Meridian with the unedited voyage: the purge, the names, the children's true ages. Vey's override fails because thousands of witnesses now share the memory. Beat: cathartic climax, truth as something held collectively rather than owned.

chapters.title: Ledger
chapters.summary: POV Astrid. Months later, Meridian rebuilds around a new archive honoring the erased. Astrid has lost his childhood memories but kept his purpose; Okafor, aging forward again, becomes his archivist. He cannot recall his mother's face but reads her letters daily. Beat: bittersweet resolution, belonging earned through shared remembrance.
